items.title: 68146_Russell Procope oral history interview
items.q: Sam Wooding said the same thing.

ctx.x: But I remember Elmer Snowden telling me about, you know, the blues singers and people who came up from the south. Musically he didn't think very much of them, you know. Sam Wooding said the same thing. He thought Bessie Smith, for instance, and all those blues singers, they were so slow, he said Bessie would start a verse and he'd go to the bathroom and when he came back she was just finishing the same verse, you know, she was so slow. And Howard Scott said the

same thing, that he didn't really -- it bored him to accompany blues singers because it was all very monotonous, very much the same and very simplistic music. And I've always sensed that maybe there was a little bit of snobbery there by New York musicians, thinking that the people from the south were a little bit primitive.
